# Agent environments

## What an environment is
State, observations, actions, dynamics. The reward is a separate claim about what matters.

## Partial observability (POMDP)
When the agent cannot see the full state it must maintain a belief and sometimes act to gather information. Measurement can be an action with a cost.

## Attention as a hidden variable
Learners do not read everything shown to them. Attention gates learning and drains with fatigue.

We evaluate reliability using pass^k across at least 3 random seeds. pass@k asks whether at least one of k runs succeeds, but pass^k asks whether all k runs succeed, so it is stricter and better matches deployment reliability. ## Environment definition
Environment = state, observations, actions, and dynamics.
- State: underlying world variables relevant to the task, including files/calendar and possibly hidden variables like student attention.
- Observations: what the agent can see, such as messages, assignment text, notes, calendar events, and quiz results.
- Actions: operations the agent can take, such as opening readings, sending messages, quizzing, editing notes, and scheduling study blocks.
- Dynamics: how the state changes after actions and over time, e.g. reading can improve knowledge, quizzes reveal understanding, attention can drop with fatigue, and time passing changes deadlines and memory.

args.text:
## Polished version

### Environment definition
The agent’s environment consists of state, observations, actions, and dynamics. The state includes the underlying task variables: files, calendar, note contents, current time and deadline, and hidden student variables such as knowledge and attention. The observations are the parts of that state the agent can actually see, including assignment text, messages, visible notes, calendar events, and quiz results. The actions are the operations available to the agent, such as opening readings, sending messages, running quizzes, editing notes, adding study blocks, and waiting. The dynamics describe how the state changes over time and after actions: reading and feedback can improve knowledge, quizzes reveal understanding, deadlines get closer, and attention can decrease with fatigue and recover with rest.

### Evaluation
We evaluate the agent using pass^k over at least three seeds. pass@k counts a task as successful if at least one of k runs succeeds, while pass^k requires all k runs to succeed. Because this build is about reliability rather than one lucky run, pass^k is the better metric. In the write-up, report the result for at least three seeds and briefly summarize how consistently the agent succeeds across runs.
